skills.description: Combine and correct counts in a sample.
Share a sample total equally across observations.
Express a part of a sample out of one hundred.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Using the number of groups as the total.
Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.
Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: Two classes bring 6 and 4 seeds. How many seeds did they bring altogether?
hints: Combine the two class counts.
questions.explanation: Combine the two class counts. The calculation is 6+4 = 10.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: A shelf has 9 storybooks. A pupil adds 3. How many are there now?
hints: Start with the books already on the shelf.
questions.explanation: Start with the books already on the shelf. The calculation is 9+3 = 12.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: A total of 8 cards is shared equally between 2 groups. How many per group?
hints: Share the total into equal groups.
questions.explanation: Share the total into equal groups. The calculation is 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: A hundred-square has 20 shaded squares. What percentage is shaded?
hints: The whole grid has exactly one hundred squares.
questions.explanation: The whole grid has exactly one hundred squares. The calculation is 20 ÷ 100 × 100 = 20%.
questions.misconception: Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: Five pupils walk and five cycle. How many journeys were recorded?
hints: Both groups made journeys.
questions.explanation: Both groups made journeys. The calculation is 5+5 = 10.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: Three pupils read 2, 4 and 6 pages. What is their average number of pages?
hints: Count the readers before sharing the total.
questions.explanation: Count the readers before sharing the total. The calculation is (2+4+6) ÷ 3 = 4.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: The class counted 8, 11 and 6 seedlings in three rows. Find the total.
hints: Include each row once.
questions.explanation: Include each row once. The calculation is 8+11+6 = 25.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: Five out of ten pupils choose football. What percentage chose football?
hints: Write the part as a share of the full group.
questions.explanation: Write the part as a share of the full group. The calculation is 5 ÷ 10 × 100 = 50%.
questions.misconception: Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: Two teams collected 9 and 15 bottles. What was the average per team?
hints: Think about making the two piles equal.
questions.explanation: Think about making the two piles equal. The calculation is (9+15) ÷ 2 = 12.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: A survey has responses on three sheets: 12, 8 and 7. How many responses is that?
hints: Combine the sheet counts.
questions.explanation: Combine the sheet counts. The calculation is 12+8+7 = 27.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: One of four equal parts of a class chart is green. What percentage is green?
hints: Imagine splitting one hundred squares equally into four sets.
questions.explanation: Imagine splitting one hundred squares equally into four sets. The calculation is 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25%.
questions.misconception: Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: The school recorded 3 visitors on Monday, 6 on Tuesday and 9 on Wednesday. What was the daily average?
hints: Use the number of days as your divisor.
questions.explanation: Use the number of days as your divisor. The calculation is (3+6+9) ÷ 3 = 6.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: A basket count of 14 includes two spoiled oranges. Another basket has 9 good oranges. Find the total number of good oranges.
hints: Work out the good count in the first basket before combining.
questions.explanation: Work out the good count in the first basket before combining. The calculation is 14-2+9 = 21.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: A pupil wrote 8 instead of 5 in the list 4, 8, 9. After correcting the list, what is the mean?
hints: Replace the wrong entry before finding the total.
questions.explanation: Replace the wrong entry before finding the total. The calculation is (4+5+9) ÷ 3 = 6.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: Of 20 seedlings, 4 have no leaves yet. What percentage have leaves?
hints: Count those with leaves first.
questions.explanation: Count those with leaves first. The calculation is (20-4) ÷ 20 × 100 = 80%.
questions.misconception: Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: Two pupils counted the same four exercise books twice in a total of 23. What is the corrected total?
hints: Remove just the extra count.
questions.explanation: Remove just the extra count. The calculation is 23-4 = 19.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.

questions.stem: A bus carried 8, 12 and 16 pupils on three trips. What equally sized group per trip would give the same total?
hints: Use all three trips.
questions.explanation: Use all three trips. The calculation is (8+12+16) ÷ 3 = 12.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: Ten pupils answered yesterday and ten today. Three yesterday and seven today chose mangoes. What percentage of all respondents chose mangoes?
hints: Combine both the chosen counts and the group sizes.
questions.explanation: Combine both the chosen counts and the group sizes. The calculation is (3+7) ÷ (10+10) × 100 = 50%.
questions.misconception: Using the part as the whole when finding a percentage.

questions.stem: Two gardens have 8 and 10 plants. A third has 15, but 3 are counted twice. Find the average number of plants per garden after correction.
hints: Correct the third count before sharing among the gardens.
questions.explanation: Correct the third count before sharing among the gardens. The calculation is (8+10+15-3) ÷ 3 = 10.
questions.misconception: Sharing by the largest observation instead of the number of observations.

questions.stem: Six pairs counted three shells per pair. A teacher adds seven more, then takes away one that was already recorded. What total should be entered?
hints: Count the pairs first and apply both corrections.
questions.explanation: Count the pairs first and apply both corrections. The calculation is 6 × 3+7-1 = 24.
questions.misconception: Using the number of groups as the total.
